analysis.one_liner: Cuts acid rain pollution from power plants while paying utilities' cleanup costs with a fee on electricity.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have cut power plant sulfur dioxide pollution by 10 million tons a year, never received a hearing or vote and died in committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Air Act to force a two-phase, ten-year reduction of sulfur dioxide from power plants — 10 million tons a year below 1980 levels — plus a 2-million-ton cut in nitrogen oxides. States would have written compliance plans, with public input on costs, and utilities could trade emissions reductions among plants. The catch: electricity customers would pay a fee of up to 1 mill per kilowatt-hour to fund a federal treasury that reimburses utilities for up to 90% of the cost of scrubbers and clean coal equipment, and the bill included special protections to keep utilities burning high-sulfur coal.
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to acid rain and power plant pollution — downwind communities, lake and forest ecosystems, and anyone who breathes air affected by coal-plant emissions. Utilities and coal producers also benefit from the subsidies, compliance deadlines extensions, and contract protections built into the bill.

how_it_helps.text: Would cut annual sulfur dioxide emissions from power plants by 10 million tons below 1980 levels over ten years, and nitrogen oxides by 2 million tons below 1985 levels [S2][S3].
Requires states to make cost and employment impact information public for comment before adopting final control plans, and to include ratepayers in plan development [S2][S3].
Requires power plants and major emissions sources to keep emissions records and make them available to the public [S2][S3].
Allows utilities to meet part of their cleanup obligation through energy conservation programs instead of new equipment, and gives states flexibility in how reductions are achieved [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Electricity customers, through a fee of up to 1 mill per kilowatt-hour on fossil fuel generation and imported electricity, and taxpayers, through Department of Energy payment of retrofit costs at three federally connected power plants and a grants program covering up to half the cost of clean coal technology.

drawbacks.text: The bill would impose a fee of up to 1.0 mill per kilowatt-hour on electric generation, a cost utilities would pass through to their customers [S2][S3].

The fee-funded fund pays utilities up to 90% of their capital costs for scrubbers and clean coal technology — public money cushioning the polluting industry, with the stated intent that states whose ratepayers pay into the fund get payments back out [S3].

A force majeure clause prohibits utilities from terminating coal supply contracts because of the new rules, explicitly to prevent coal miner unemployment — locking utilities into high-sulfur coal and raising compliance costs that ratepayers ultimately bear [S3].

The bill allows small power plants to be exempted from reductions if their compliance costs would significantly exceed the state average, and gives utilities up to five extra years to comply if they commit to clean coal technology — carve-outs that dilute the total reduction [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The emissions cuts themselves were large and would have addressed acid rain, a serious environmental problem damaging lakes, forests, and buildings across the Northeast. But the bill's design leans heavily toward protecting the coal and utility industries: ratepayers pay a fee, much of which flows back to the utilities as subsidies, while contract protections keep the highest-sulfur coal in use. An honest supporter would acknowledge that some of the money extracted from the public would have gone to cushioning industry rather than maximizing cleanup.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to two of its subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Glenn Poshard (D-IL) introduced the bill on September 21, 1989, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S1][S5].
On October 20, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power and the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment; no further action was ever taken on the bill [S5].
The bill never attracted a single cosponsor [S4].
The Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill died without a markup, floor vote, or companion action in the Senate [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Utilities and the high-sulfur coal industry were better off, at least for a year — they avoided the new fee, the compliance mandates, and the limits on coal contract terminations. The larger acid rain fight was settled soon after: Congress passed comparable sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide reductions in the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments, signed into law in November 1990, using a different cap-and-trade design that gave utilities more flexibility than this bill's fee-and-fund approach.

for.name: Rep. Glenn Poshard
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made the case for cutting acid rain pollution while protecting the coal industry; the bill drew no cosponsors.

against.name: John Dingell
against.role: Chairman, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee referred the bill to subcommittees, where it was never scheduled for a hearing or markup, keeping it off the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support for this particular bill was never tested; broader acid rain legislation in the same Congress drew opposition from coal-state members of both parties.

industries.note: The bill's stated purposes include ensuring the survival of the coal industry: it prohibits utilities from terminating coal supply contracts due to the new rules and steers compliance toward clean coal technology grants, keeping high-sulfur coal in use even as emissions are cut. Those protections raise compliance costs that electricity customers ultimately pay.

Utilities face emission limits and a generation fee, but receive payments covering up to 90% of scrubber and clean coal capital costs, can trade emissions reductions among plants, get up to five-year extensions for clean coal commitments, and small plants can be exempted. The bill also requires DOE to pay retrofit costs at three federally connected plants.

industries.industry: Pollution control equipment and clean coal technology vendors
industries.note: The bill creates a federal fund and a seven-year grant program paying for installation of scrubbers, nitrogen oxide controls, and new clean coal technologies, up to half of capital costs — a mandate-plus-subsidy structure that guarantees these firms customers.
